extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, compositors, copyholders and printers involved in book and journal production
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for typesetting (tables, spacing, indentation, headings), manuscript preparation, proof correction, and the duties/techniques of proofreaders and copyholders in book production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table captions and box-heads sizing and case
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for the columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ruled tables with box-heads of several stories, the upper story (primary heads) should be set in caps and small caps, except where the second story consists of figures only; the lower (secondary) in caps and lower-case. Wherever small caps are used in box-heads, the stub (first column) head should, as a rule, also be set in caps and small caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between rules and table matter (leads and quads)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and, if practicable, at least the equivalent of an en-quad of the type in which the body of the table is set, between the perpendicular rules and the matter inclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minimum two-lead spacing above/below horizontal rules; where possible leave an en-quad between perpendicular rules and enclosed matter to provide proper separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leaders and periods between table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders, may be used between the columns. In ruled tables, in the 'stub,' leaders should usually be employed, if there is room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A leader is a piece of type with dots (period leader) or short lines (hyphen leader) used to lead the eye across a space to the right word or number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing blanks in figure columns with leaders and centering figures
rubrics_metrics.description: In columns of figures, to express a blank use leaders the width of the largest number in the column; e.g., for four digits use a 2-em leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each em contains two dots; never use less than two dots. Center figures in the column; if exact centering is impossible and digit-groups are unequal, leave more space on the left than on the right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-matter in ruled-table columns alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered, if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention, and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center when feasible; handle wrap/overflow with hanging indent so that continued lines align left within the column.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of double rules in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables, but perpendicularly, as a usual thing, only when a table is doubled up on itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply vertical double rules sparingly—generally only for doubled tables—while always placing double rules atop tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs ruled table rule by column count
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of two columns only should be set as open; of three or more, as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-table format for two-column tables; apply ruled format when three or more columns are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table headlines and numbering typography
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I,' etc., in headlines of tables should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following (descriptive) line, if any, in caps and small caps of the same type. A single (descriptive) headline, not preceded by the number of the table, should be set in caps of the type in which the table is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number line use same type caps as table body; descriptive line in caps & small caps; if unnumbered, set single headline in caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the point/pica system
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica. A pica is twelve points (one-sixth of an inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common point sizes (12-pt pica, 11-pt small pica, 10-pt long primer, 9-pt bourgeois, 8-pt brevier, 7-pt minion, 6-pt nonpareil, 5-pt pearl) are the sizes usually used in book composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype vs linotype spacing systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotype composition uses an 18-unit unit-system in quads with fixed cast spaces (6-unit = 3-em, 5-unit = 4-em etc.), while linotype uses the pica system with three fixed spaces (em-quad, en-quad, thin space) and a space band to spread spaces between sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotype has fixed cast spaces and 'swelling' (justifying) space spread by keyboard instruction; linotype spreads spaces with a space band (between 3-em and slightly larger than an en-quad); spaces smaller than a thin space must be put in by hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of em, en, quads, and related spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: An em (em-quad) is a square block used as a unit; an en-quad is half its width. A three-em space is one-third of an em and is the standard space used to separate words. Jour-em, five-em, middle, thin, and hair-spaces defined similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two- and three-em quads, em- and en-dashes, and the appearance of various space widths are defined for consistent typographic measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space evenly — standard interword and punctuation spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard line should have a 3-em space between all words not separated by other punctuation points than commas, and after commas; an en-quad after semicolons, and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em-quad after periods, and exclamation and interrogation points, concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these specific space widths after different punctuation marks to maintain even spacing and typographic consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for reducing or increasing spacing in a line
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary to reduce spacing in a line, begin with commas, and letters of slanting form; if necessary to increase, begin with overlapping letters (kerns), straight-up-and-down letters, and points other than periods and commas (in this order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust spacing first at characters least perceptible when changed (commas, slanted letters) and expand at characters that better hide added space (kerned, vertical letters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion rule for well-spaced lines
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line, with a 3-em space between a majority of the words, there should not be more than an en-quad between the rest; this proportion should be maintained in increasing or reducing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the proportion so that most spaces are the standard width and only a minority deviate up to an en-quad to justify lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alternating very thin and very wide spaced lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, or vice versa, if at all avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep visual rhythm across successive lines—avoid abrupt contrast in spacing that draws attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on hair-spacing or quadting to avoid run-over
rubrics_metrics.description: Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not artificially compress or expand lines (hair-spacing, em-quads) solely to prevent line breaks; use proper layout adjustments instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out last line of paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph allowing of an indention of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adding wide spaces at the end of paragraph lines that create a ragged visual end or large end-gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing around short words
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words, like 'a,' 'an,' etc., should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain equal spacing around short words to preserve even word color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thin space with section, paragraph, and metric indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, ¶, and similar signs; before 'f.,' 'ff.,' and the metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '§ 14. Be it further ordained . . .'; also examples for page and measurement notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between monetary symbol and numeral
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols $, and £ (pounds), s. (shillings), and d. (pence), and the numerals: $2.75; £10 3s. 2d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep currency symbols tight to numerals as conventional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals at line-beginnings and in headings
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines, denoting subsections, there should be an en-quad. After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of center-heads there should be an em-quad. Small-cap headings should have an en-quad between the words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply differing quad spacing depending on context (subsection label vs center-head vs heading styles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing for scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced thus: II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5—3:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow compact punctuation and spacing for biblical citations as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: No space between letters forming products and before superscripts/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nx^2 = Σm2 (v2z2 — 2vwyz + 2w*y2). Keep multiplicative and algebraic notation compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules by measure and type size
rubrics_metrics.description: In measures of less than 10 picas' width, indent all sizes 1 em; in measures of from 10 to 20, indent various sizes (11-pt 1 em; 10-pt 1½ em; 9-pt 1½; 8-pt 1½; 6-pt 2); in measures 20 to 30, indent different specific amounts (e.g., 11-pt 1½ ems; etc.). For hanging indentions, larger indents are prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified indent amounts for 'plain paragraphs' and increased indents for hanging indents depending on measure and type-size. (See section 274 for exact per-size table.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry centering and indentation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let the indention be governed by that; if the longest line is of disproportionate length, use an average of the long lines. Where quotations of different poems vary slightly, indent all alike; indent according to rhymes and length of lines; in blank verse align lines; align consecutive rhyming lines and indent alternate rhymes alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a line is disproportionately short, indent it more; examples and stanza treatments provided for practical handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs and use-cases for hanging indention
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are always preferable. Hanging indention is used to bring into relief the opening word(s) of a paragraph, the number introducing such paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to plain paragraphs; apply hanging indention only for emphasis or typographic necessity (e.g., long center-heads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of leads and slugs
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary (standard) lead is 2 points thick. A slug is a strip of metal thicker than a lead used in make-up; standard sizes are 6 and 12 points thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter with leads is 'leaded'; without is 'solid'. Use leads/slugs consistently in make-up to control vertical spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-heads, side-heads, cut-in heads, box-heads, running-heads formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Center-heads are headlines placed at equal distances from margins, usually set in caps or small caps; where center-heads exceed line counts use pyramid form (2–3 lines) or hanging indention (more than three). Side-heads may be set flush or run-in, frequently in italics with only the first word and proper names capitalized; sometimes in caps & small caps or bold-face. A cut-in head is set in a box cut into the side of the type-page; a box-head is for a column in a ruled table. Running-heads are placed at the top of each page giving main title on verso and chapter title on recto; working rule—set them in roman or italic capitals two sizes smaller than text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose head style by context (center vs side vs running); apply case and sizing conventions; use pyramid or hanging formats for multi-line center-heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two paragraph kinds: plain and hanging (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain (regular) paragraph has the first line indented and the others set flush. A hanging paragraph ('hanging indention') has the first line set flush and the others indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain paragraphs normally; employ hanging paragraphs when typographically or contextually required (e.g., long heads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of proof types (galley, page, plate, foul, revise)
rubrics_metrics.description: A galley-proof is an impression of type in a galley; a page-proof is an impression made up into page-form; a plate-proof or foundry-proof is a proof taken immediately before an electrotype cast is made (has black border); a foul proof is a galley-proof containing author's corrections; a revise is a new proof corrected from a marked proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand each proof stage and its role in production; plate proofs relate to electrotypes and are used where printing from plates occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up and folio definitions and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: The arranging into page-form of type-lines is called the make-up. A folio is a page-number (even on verso, odd on recto). A hall-title (bastard title) is abbreviated title placed on a separate page preceding full title or a part/chapter title preceding that part on its own page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow conventions for folio placement and include hall-title where appropriate in book preliminaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotype and linotype machine descriptions and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The monotype composes by perforated paper and casting characters separately on a galley (unit system); the linotype composes matrices arranged as lines and casts slugs each consisting of a line of type (pica system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize operational differences: monotype allows easier single-number changes; linotype may require resetting entire lines/series when numbers change—this affects decisions like footnote numbering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript preparation: legibility, paper, and fastening
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be typewritten or in perfectly clear handwriting (typewritten preferable). Sheets should be uniform size (9"x11" desirable). Only one side should be used. Never roll manuscripts; place flat in a box or envelope. Sheets should not be fastened together except by pins or clips easily removed. When fastening one piece of a page to another, use mucilage, not pins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare manuscripts to facilitate handling and reduce risk of damage/loss; avoid folding/rolling and use removable fastenings; use mucilage for inserts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript margins and pagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberal margins should be left at the top and left-hand side of the sheets for reader/printer directions. The pages should be numbered consecutively. Inserted and omitted pages should be clearly indicated (e.g., '4A', '4B', or '4–7'). Additions should be placed after the sheets to which they belong and marked 'Insert A', 'Insert B'; indicate insertion point by writing 'Here insert A' on the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide margin space for notes; use clear, consistent labeling for page inserts/omissions to avoid misplacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and footnote marking in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated, either by indenting the first line or by a ¶ mark. Footnotes should be clearly designated, separated from the text by a running line or different color ink; the word in the text carrying the note should be followed by a superior figure corresponding to that preceding the note. Footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep footnotes distinct and consistently numbered; avoid in-text parenthetical footnotes in manuscripts to prevent confusion in make-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote numbering practice considering linotype resetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because in matter set on the linotype the slightest change necessitates resetting of the whole line and renumbering notes is impracticable, the best way is to number them consecutively throughout an article or by chapters in a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number notes consecutively across the article or by chapter to minimize resetting work on linotype; monotype/hand-set matter can handle local numbering changes more easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and returning proofs promptly and answering queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return your proofs promptly. In marking proof-sheets, use the standard proofreaders' marks. Be careful to answer all queries in the proofs; delays and errors often result from not attending to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt proof return reduces errors and costs; always respond to compositor queries to clarify ambiguous matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize corrections and avoid plate corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that changes in the type cost money; make your manuscript as perfect as possible before delivering it to the printer. Any necessary alterations should be made in the galley-proof, as each succeeding stage will add to the cost. Corrections in plates should be studiously avoided because they are expensive and apt to injure the plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit corrections after page proofs and avoid plate corrections; prefer making changes earlier (manuscript/galley) to control expense and damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return and accompany proofs with original/previous marked sets
rubrics_metrics.description: The original manuscript should in each instance be returned with the galley-proof so the proofreader may refer to it; each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply prior marked proofs with each submission to help calculate alteration costs and clarify changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreaders: overall responsibility and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything as if you yourself were the author. Be particularly careful about proper names and figures. Do not follow copy blindly, unreasoningly. Follow copy only when, and as far as, it is correct. The proofreader is the judge; do not ask authors or editors to decide questions of style—the Manual of Style is primarily meant for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take responsibility for typographical correctness; correct palpable errors even when copy asserts otherwise; do not defer stylistic judgments to authors/editors when rules exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreaders: querying, discretion, and personal equation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the copy is not perfectly clear, or if you have reason to doubt its correctness, look it up, or query the author. In asking questions of authors or editors, make your point clear. Be discreet about your queries and study the 'personal equation' of individuals with whom you deal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make queries specific and non-trivial; adapt query style to the preferences of recurring contacts; avoid asking foolish/trivial questions on proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreaders: handling rush work and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: In unavoidable cases of 'rush' protect yourself by letting it be understood that you have done your best in the time allotted you, but that you must disclaim any further responsibility. Put your initial at the top of every galley you read or revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document rushed conditions and initial work to record responsibility and facilitate tracing of corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholders: reading technique and collaboration with proofreader
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading-voice; small words are as essential as big ones; enunciate plural 's's distinctly. Do not keep guessing at a word—look closely and consider context; sit at right angles to the reader if possible; give the reader time to make corrections and evolve an internal code of signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient vocalization and synchronized signals between copyholder and reader speed proofreading while reducing errors; do not waste time on style matters the proofreader is expected to know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholders: organization and sending proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not waste time over matters of style; be careful in transferring marks. In sending out proofs, see that everything is there—arrange copy and proof-sheets neatly and consecutively. The manuscript should accompany the galley-proof; the foul proof should accompany the page-proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain organized packaging and correct accompaniment of materials to prevent omissions and delays; fasten pins center at top to avoid covering directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housekeeping of the proof-room and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that you are the housekeeper of the proof-room; keep records, files, etc., so that everything can be located at a moment's notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and perfect systems of storage and record-keeping; the more you do proactively, the more appreciated you will be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard proofreader's marks and place initial on work
rubrics_metrics.description: In marking proof-sheets, use the standard proofreaders' marks. Put your initial at the top of every galley you read or revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inventing ad-hoc marks; use accepted marks (delete, transpose, indent, carry left/right, shove down, restore words, etc.) so compositors understand corrections. Initials assist tracing and credit.
